nameStory: The thick-legged jumping spider earned its common name from its noticeably robust, chunky legs that set it apart from its more slender-legged jumping spider cousins. This spider was named after William Morton Wheeler, a renowned entomologist who made significant contributions to the study of social insects and spiders in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
description: The thick-legged jumping spider is a compact, sturdy member of the jumping spider family found across northern New England. Like all jumping spiders, it has excellent vision and hunts by stalking and pouncing on prey rather than building webs. These spiders are small but muscular, with particularly robust legs that give them their distinctive appearance. They're active hunters that you might spot sunning themselves on rocks, logs, or tree bark during warm days.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, chunky build with a noticeably thick, robust appearance compared to other jumping spiders; feels solid and heavy for its size

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Legs are unusually thick and powerful-looking, especially the front pair used for grasping prey; they feel sturdy rather than delicate when observed

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes in a characteristic jumping spider arrangement, with the two central eyes noticeably larger and giving an almost curious expression

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with deliberate stops; will turn to face you directly when approached, often tilting its body to get a better look

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small but stocky, typically fitting comfortably on a fingernail with legs extended; appears more substantial than most other jumping spiders of similar length

habitat: Look for thick-legged jumping spiders in northern New England's mixed forests, particularly on sun-warmed surfaces like fallen logs, tree bark, and rocky outcrops. They prefer areas with dappled sunlight where they can hunt actively during the day. You're most likely to spot them in mature forests with plenty of dead wood and varied microclimates.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots under bark and begin active hunting as temperatures warm, often seen sunbathing on south-facing surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults hunting actively during warm days and mating season occurring; look for them most easily during sunny morning hours.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue hunting until the first hard frosts, when they seek protected overwintering sites under loose bark or in rock crevices.
seasonality.winter: Hidden in protected spots under bark, logs, or rock piles in a state of dormancy; rarely seen unless you disturb their hiding places on warm winter days.

funFact: Despite being called jumping spiders, they don't actually leap blindly - they trail a safety line of silk behind them like a bungee cord, so if they miss their target or need to escape quickly, they can rappel to safety like tiny eight-legged rock climbers!
confusionNotes: With only one confirmed observation in New England, this spider could easily be mistaken for other robust jumping spiders, particularly bold jumping spiders or wolf spiders. The key difference is the eye arrangement - jumping spiders have four large front eyes in a square pattern, while wolf spiders have eyes in three distinct rows. Memory trick: jumping spiders look like they're wearing glasses with their big front eyes.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only a single recorded observation, making it more of a northern species that just barely reaches into our region. Most jumping spider sightings in New England will be other, more common species, so consider this a special find if you encounter one.
compareHints: The thick-legged jumping spider differs from its close relative, the thin-legged jumping spider (Admestina tibialis), primarily in its more robust leg structure and stockier overall build. While both are northern species with similar habitats, the thick-legged variety has a more muscular appearance throughout its body. Within the jumping spider family in New England, this species stands out for its particularly robust build compared to the more common bold jumping spiders or bronze jumping spiders.
